chapter_theme: Neythal: the heroine and her friend on the shore of backwaters and screw-pine, complaining of trysts that proved false and of pallor and slipping bangles, pressing the sea lord to come and marry (41-48, 50); and the man's first-sight doubt whether the girl of the njazhal grove is peacock, woman or sea goddess (49).

41.reading: The heroine tells her friend that the lord of the cool shore, with its neythal gardens and brimming backwaters, is no longer as he was the day she first saw him in the screw-pine-ringed seaside grove; the trysts he set have proved false, and she asks whether the bond of the noble is really so frail.
41.nuance: ஐயகொல் ஆன்றார் தொடர்பு turns a maxim into a reproach: she does not say he lied, but asks whether the bond of the worthy (ஆன்றார்) is so slight, which quietly puts him outside that class. The first sight in the grove (கண்டநாள்) is the measure he has fallen from.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal-flowered shore, the backwater and the seaside grove

42.reading: The friend asks the lord of the cool sea shore, where the old bent-trunked punnai puts out buds like pearls and the leaping waves heave, to grant his grace to the girl who is like a painted flowering creeper: his chest with its fine green ornaments.
42.nuance: What the friend asks him to give is his chest (மார்பு), so arul here is not pity but the embrace and the claim it makes; the plea for grace is a plea for him to take her openly.

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai of the shore and the sea-lord

comparisons.tenor: the heroine, slender and bright as a painted flowering creeper
the punnai buds, white and round as pearls

43.reading: The friend tells the heroine, girl of fine jewels whose sweet speech never parts from good sense, that the trysts set by the lord of the long backwater, where the tide of the shark-tossed sea moves and prawns wheel along their path, never lose their closeness with her.
43.nuance: நின்னில் செறிவுஅறா செய்த குறி can also mean that the marks of their meetings never leave her body, so that the friend has guessed the secret (an opening of the friend's discovery) rather than reassured her. The striking shark beside the wheeling prawns invites a hidden reading, but it gives only a mood, not two pairs, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the long sea and its backwater

44.reading: The friend asks the lord of the ford, where the tide with its young fish moves over the dark backwater and gem-clear water spreads, whether it is fitting for him to stay away from the side of the creeper-like girl whose good nature never fails, without even the grace of thinking of her.
44.nuance: The verse plays on நீர் three ways: the gem-clear water (மணிநீர்), her unfailing nature (குணநீர்மை) and his lack of the nature of remembering (நினைநீர்மை). Her constancy is set against his forgetting in the same word.

comparisons.tenor: the heroine, slender as a creeper

45.reading: The friend tells the lord of the ford, where fishermen's daughters with jewelled girdles on hood-shaped hips string into garlands the bright pearls the sea has washed up and heaped, and play, of the sickness that has entered her friend's body.
45.nuance: The playing girls who make ornaments of what the sea gives freely stand against the friend's girl, who is ill; the contrast is left unstated. The last line has no finite verb (உரைத்து), so the friend's message is cut off at 'telling of her sickness'.

thinai_evidence.note: the fisherfolk and the pearls the sea casts up

comparisons.tenor: the girls' hips, broad as a snake's jewelled hood

46.reading: The friend tells the lord of the curving backwater, where flocks of herons cry on the wide shore of the fragrant seaside grove, that he must come to join her for good, so that the sickness he caused, which wastes her beauty, may end.
46.nuance: மருவி வரல் asks for a coming that stays, not another visit, so the plea is for marriage; and உன்நோய், 'your sickness', lays the girl's illness at his door.

thinai_evidence.note: the seaside grove and the curving backwater

47.reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the lord of the shore of the surging sea has abandoned her, now that she is not as she was that day in the lovely flowered grove by the backwater: pallor spreads like flowers over her gem-bright body and the bangles slip down her soft shoulders.
47.nuance: அற்றைநாள் போலான, 'not as on that day', is the same measure as in verse 41, but here it is her own body, not his conduct, that has changed; the question துறந்தான்கொல் she cannot answer reads itself on her skin.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater grove and the sea-lord

48.reading: As the tall chariot with ringing bells cuts its way, crabs scatter over the gleaming sand and the fierce sun that parches hurries away, the evening, deepening in colour, comes on.
48.nuance: The speaker is not named, and the chariot can be the man's coming at dusk (a hope) or the sun's own car leaving (a dread of evening). கண்வாள் அறுப்ப is obscure: the wheel's blade-like rim cutting the sand is the likeliest sense.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore sand at sunset, neythal's hour

49.reading: The man, struck at first sight, asks his companions whether she was a peacock, a young woman, or a goddess dwelling in the waves of the great sea, for his heart aches from the eyes that looked at him by the flowering grove of young njazhal where the koel calls.
49.nuance: This is the first-sight doubt (ஐயம்) of kalavu, and the shore supplies its goddess: not the hill's anangu but one who lives in the waves. The pain is placed in her look (நோக்கிய கண்ணின்), not her beauty.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea-goddess of the waves and the njazhal grove of the shore

comparisons.vehicle: மயில்கொல் மடவாள்கொல் மாநீர்த் திரையுள் பயில்வதோர் தெய்வம்கொல்
comparisons.tenor: the girl he saw, whom he cannot place as bird, woman or goddess

50.reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the lord of the shore of creeping waves, his bright chest where Tiru dwells, will come to their front yard, where coral, pearls and crystal, mixed together, are brought as if in praise and heaped up at the edge.
50.nuance: Who heaps the gems is not said (the waves, or the fisherfolk), and புகழக் கொணர்ந்து makes it an offering. A reader may hear in the treasure piled at her door the bride-wealth she hopes he will bring, but the act is not tied to him, so it is left as scene rather than iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: the wave-washed shore and its house-front

links.note: Kural 782: the friendship of the worthy grows like the waxing moon. Thinaimozhi 41: the worthy man's bond has waned since the day she saw him, and his trysts proved false; on a plain reading the heroine's case contradicts the maxim.
links.teaches: The heroine's question ஐயகொல் ஆன்றார் தொடர்பு tests the Kural's rule against one man and finds it failing, so the akam poem uses the ethical maxim as a weapon: either the rule is wrong or he was never one of the worthy.

links.note: Natrinai 11: the friend tells the heroine, wilting since the tryst he set failed (அவர் செய் குறி பிழைப்ப), to drop the resentful thought that he will not come, for his charioteer is driving along the moonlit shore sparing the crabs. Thinaimozhi 41 is that resentful thought spoken: his trysts have turned false (செய்த குறியும்பொய் யாயின).
links.teaches: Held together the two give the complaint and its answer in one neythal exchange: the venba lets the heroine conclude from the failed tryst that his bond is false, while the older poem shows the friend refusing that inference and offering his gentleness on the road as proof.

links.note: Kuruntokai 121: the heroine grants her friend that for the hill man's failure to keep the tryst (தான்குறி வாயாத் தப்பற்கு) her own shoulders have turned pale, as the branch goes down with the langur that missed its leap. Thinaimozhi 41: for the same failure she questions his nobility.
links.teaches: The same failed tryst draws two answers from the heroine: in the Kuruntokai she takes the fault into her own body, while the later venba turns it outward into a charge against his worth, which shows accusation as a second, sharper register of the same situation.

links.note: Kural 1234: with the partner gone, the shoulders lose their old beauty and fullness and the bright bangles slip. Thinaimozhi 47: the heroine asks her friend whether he has abandoned her, as pallor spreads and the bangles of her soft shoulders slip.
links.teaches: The couplet states the sign as a fact of separation, while the venba makes the heroine read it as a question, has he left me?, so the slipping bangle becomes the evidence by which she learns his desertion rather than its mere effect.

links.note: Akananuru 260 lists the signs of evening on the neythal shore (the sun dimming, herons crying, the crab slipping into its hole, the waves falling quiet) before the heroine asks what will become of her. Thinaimozhi 48 gives a chariot cutting the sand, crabs scattering and the sun hurrying away as the evening comes.
links.teaches: The long poem shows that the neythal evening was built as a catalogue of shore signs ending in the heroine's dread, which lets the four-line venba keep only three signs and the bare 'evening will come' and still carry that dread unstated.

links.note: Kural 1081: on first seeing her the man asks whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman, and his heart reels. Thinaimozhi 49: the man asks whether she was a peacock, a young woman or a goddess of the sea waves, and his heart aches from her eyes.
links.teaches: The same three-way doubt in both shows the first-sight ஐயம் was a fixed form of kalavu, and the venba adds what the couplet leaves open: a place for the seeing, the njazhal grove, and a goddess native to that place, the one who lives in the waves.

links.note: Akananuru 282: the father agrees to give the girl to the hill lord whose hunters bring ivory, gold, gems and pearls together, and the household prays for the wedding day. Thinaimozhi 50: the heroine asks whether the sea lord will come to the front yard where coral, pearls and crystal are heaped as if in praise.
links.teaches: Akananuru 282 makes the suitor's treasure of the land the very thing that wins the father's consent, so beside it the shore's coral, pearls and crystal piled at the heroine's door read as the bride-wealth her question 'will he come?' is waiting for.

source_issues.issue: The text flag says sangamtamil.com lacks this verse; our text cannot be checked against that witness.
குருதினம் (line 2) is probably a misprint for குருகினம், 'flock of herons', the form Akananuru 260.3 has in the same shore scene; read as such.
தணியும்எள் (line 4) is probably a misprint for தணியும்என், 'my (shoulders)'; read as such.
Line 4 ends on the non-finite உரைத்து with no main verb, so the verse reads as incomplete or elliptical.
